slides.html:
What Are We Trying to Answer?

Goal: turn raw data into knowledge for better decisions

  • Who will buy? How much?
  • Is this email spam?
  • What kinds of customers do we have?
  • What happens if we raise the price 5%?

One thread: generalization

How much should the model "wiggle"? Too little → bias; too much → variance. Always test on data not used in fitting.

1. Prediction and Generalization

KNN, bias–variance, cross-validation
slides.title: 1. Prediction and Generalization

slides.html:
Parametric vs Nonparametric

Parametric: assume a form (e.g. linear), estimate a few parameters.

Nonparametric: the function is defined by an algorithm on the data.

KNN:

\hat f(x^\star)=\frac1K\sum_{x_i\in\mathcal N_K(x^\star)}y_i

How to choose K? Small K → jagged (noise as signal); large K → too smooth (real wiggles erased).
slides.title: Parametric vs Nonparametric

slides.html:
In-Sample vs Out-of-Sample

  • Training error falls monotonically with complexity (zero at K=1) — it memorizes noise
  • What matters is out-of-sample RMSE:
    \mathrm{RMSE}_{\mathrm{out}}=\sqrt{\tfrac1M\textstyle\sum_{i}\big(y_i^\star-\hat f(x_i^\star)\big)^2}
  • Train/test split: the test set must not influence the fit

In-sample error is an overly optimistic estimate of future performance.
slides.title: In-Sample vs Out-of-Sample

LOOCV vs K-Fold

Bias Variance Cost
Train/test split overestimates error large small
K-fold (5–10) slight smaller medium
LOOCV nearly unbiased training sets overlap heavily large

Estimating "test error" has its own bias–variance trade-off.
slides.title: LOOCV vs K-Fold

slides.html:
The Bootstrap

Nonparametric bootstrap: draw N pairs (x_i,y_i) with replacement, refit, repeat B times.

  • Standard error = sd of \hat f^{(b)}(x)
  • Confidence interval = quantiles
Bootstrap Randomness from
Nonparametric the sample itself
Residual noise (x fixed)
Parametric parametric law

3. Linear Models and Feature Engineering

Better features almost always beat better models
slides.title: 3. Linear Models and Feature Engineering

slides.html:
Linear Models: Pros and Cons

Pros

  • Often predicts well
  • Low variance, interpretable
  • Very cheap to compute

Cons

  • Almost always "wrong" (bias)
  • Needs hand work: dummies, transformations, interactions
slides.title: Linear Models: Pros and Cons
Transformations: Pick the Scale of Linearity

slides.html:
Dummies and Interactions

Dummies: category → 0/1 columns; one baseline, other coefficients are "differences from baseline".

Interaction:

\beta_0+\beta_1x_1+\beta_2x_2+\beta_{12}x_1x_2
Effect of x_1 is \beta_1+\beta_{12}x_2.

The "effect" of a high gear depends on the road — a feature's effect depends on context.
slides.title: Dummies and Interactions

slides.html:
The KNN Trap: Scale

  • A: 4 bed, 2 bath, 2200 ft²; B: 4 bed, 2 bath, 2300 ft²; C: 2 bed, 1.5 bath, 2125 ft²
  • Euclidean: d(A,B)=100, d(A,C)\approx75 → A's nearest neighbor is C!

Standardize first: \tilde x_{ij}=(x_{ij}-\bar x_j)/s_j. Any distance-based method (KNN, clustering, PCA) needs a sensible scale.
slides.title: The KNN Trap: Scale

slides.html:
4. Classification

The conditional expectation is a probability
slides.title: 4. Classification

slides.html:
LPM vs Logistic

E(y\mid x)=P(y=1\mid x)

LPM: P=x\cdot\beta — may leave [0,1].

Logistic:

P(y=1\mid x)=\frac{e^{x\cdot\beta}}{1+e^{x\cdot\beta}}
\log\tfrac p{1-p}=x\cdot\beta

e^{\beta_j} = odds ratio multiplier per unit of x_j.

Estimation: maximum likelihood

\ell(\beta)=\sum_i\big[y_ix_i\!\cdot\!\beta-\log(1+e^{x_i\cdot\beta})\big]
slides.title: LPM vs Logistic

5. Model Selection and Regularization

Make the cost of coefficients explicit
slides.title: 5. Model Selection and Regularization

slides.html:
Why Go Beyond OLS

  • Many features, modest n → OLS variance is high; no unique solution if p>n
  • Sparse settings: many useless variables → we want automatic zeros
  • Stepwise + AIC (\text{deviance}+2p): slow and unstable
slides.title: Why Go Beyond OLS

slides.html:
Case: Partial Plus-Minus in Hockey

  • Plus/minus G_F-G_A is a marginal effect, contaminated by teammates/opponents
  • Logit per goal: player on ice for home +1, for away -1, off ice 0
  • About 69,000 goals, 2,400+ players, very sparse design matrix
  • L1 logit: most players get coefficient 0; only those with a discernible effect remain
slides.title: Case: Partial Plus-Minus in Hockey

6. Trees and Ensembles

Automatic nonlinearity and interactions
slides.title: 6. Trees and Ensembles

slides.html:
Fitting: Grow Big, Then Prune (CART)

  1. Grow: greedy recursion, each time the split that lowers loss most
  2. Prune: repeatedly remove the least useful sibling leaves, giving trees of size D,D-1,\dots,1
  3. Choose by CV (1SE rule)

Good trees are often deep → overfit, hard to interpret. Remedy: ensembles.
slides.title: Fitting: Grow Big, Then Prune (CART)

Association Rules

Measure Definition
Support \sigma(X\cup Y)/\lvert T\rvert
Confidence \sigma(X\cup Y)/\sigma(X)
Lift c(X\to Y)/s(Y)

Apriori principle: subsets of a frequent itemset are frequent; supersets of an infrequent itemset need not be counted.

Potential Outcomes and Randomized Experiments

  • \mathrm{TE}=Y_1-Y_0, only one observed → a missing-data problem
  • Needs: unconfoundedness and overlap
  • Randomize: \hat\gamma=\bar y_1-\bar y_0 is unbiased and often the best estimate

Principles to Remember

  • Evaluate out of sample; evaluation itself is noisy
  • Simplicity is a virtue: 1SE, regularization, satisficing
  • Good features beat good models; scale for distance methods
  • Choose the right tool for the problem
  • Prediction ≠ causation
  • Transparency and reproducibility

References: ISLR, ESL, Tan–Steinbach–Kumar.
